claims.text: A high-resolution microstructure-informed, physics-informed machine-learning model can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior in HfNbTiVAl10 more rapidly and accurately than established simulations.
As-fabricated HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure containing distinct dendritic and interdendritic phases or regions.
The distinct hierarchical phases in HfNbTiVAl10 govern local mechanical responses.
Spatial heterogeneity and phase distribution mediate local stress distributions in the alloy.
Detailed measurements of spatial heterogeneity and phase distribution correlate with macroscopic mechanical properties.
Features such as phase boundaries, dendrite density, and grain-size variability can help a learning model capture deformation physics more precisely.
Features such as phase boundaries, dendrite density, and grain-size variability can help a learning model capture fracture physics more precisely.
Targeted incorporation of microstructural heterogeneity can bypass some of the computational intensity of full-scale finite-element simulations.
The integrated model will be approximately 10 times faster than traditional simulations.
The integrated model will improve predictive accuracy for Young’s modulus by approximately 15–20% relative to traditional simulations.
The integrated model will improve predictive accuracy for yield strength by approximately 15–20% relative to traditional simulations.
Traditional full-scale simulations rely on averaged or less-detailed microstructural inputs.
Traditional full-scale simulations require substantially more computation time than the proposed model.
The approach may fail when imaging misses mechanically relevant small-scale heterogeneity or transient phase transformations.
The approach may fail when deformation or fracture mechanisms are not represented in the training data.
Extreme temperatures or rapid strain rates may place the material outside the model’s reliable prediction domain.
Model performance may depend on imaging resolution and the representativeness of the training data.
Independent measurements of Young’s modulus, yield strength, fracture toughness or crack-initiation stress, runtime, and prediction error can be used to test the hypothesis.
Failure to achieve at least a 10-fold runtime reduction or at least a 15% accuracy improvement across multiple independent trials will falsify the hypothesis.
